_about: Flame Atlas prepared answers (Team Flame Atlas, NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026). Answers to the questions the dashboard's buttons ask, written in advance with an AI assistant (Claude) from the team's curated NASA documents and tests table, and checked against the cited source pages in a second AI pass; same format as the live chat's answers. Every point names its source and page.

answers.question: What does the burn limit BAS-01:nodate:PMMA-ROD-DROP-BLOWOFF-FIG6.9-A142:bfe4d764 (PMMA, 16% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: Blowoff limit from 5.18-s drop-tower tests of PMMA rods in microgravity: about 16.0% final O2 at a stretch rate of about 142 s⁻¹ (the highest drop-tower blowoff), read from BAS-01 Fig. 6.9.
Method: each rod was lit in 1 g at a flammable O2 and flow, the gas switched to a lower O2 and the package dropped as it reached the flame; blowoff shows within a drop, quenching is too slow to.
Reported in BAS-01 as complementary drop tests. BAS-04 Fig. 4 shows the same point (the team's match) at about 16.0% O2 and about 141.5 s⁻¹ forced stretch, with the 0.318 cm drop blowoff marker.
The highest ISS blowoff point of Fig. 6.9 reads about 16.1% final O2 at about 150 s⁻¹; BAS-01 finds the drop-tower and ISS blowoff data agree very well.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: A drop-tower blowoff limit for PMMA rods in microgravity: in 5.18-s drops the flame blew off at about 16.0% final O2 at a stretch rate of about 142 s⁻¹.

answer.not_covered: BAS-01 prints no pressure, diluent or flow direction for these drop tests.

answers.question: What does the burn limit BAS-01:nodate:PMMA-ROD-ISS-BLOWOFF-FIG6.9-A150:667aebc8 (PMMA, 16.1% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: Blowoff limit from BAS-01 for cast PMMA rods in concurrent stagnation flow on the ISS (microgravity): about 16.1% final O2 at a stretch rate of about 150 s⁻¹ (highest-stretch ISS blowoff point, read from Fig. 6.9); pressure not reported.

Method: usually after stable burning at a modest flow, the astronaut raised the flow until blowoff, defined (Ref. 19) as the instant a hole formed in the flame at the stagnation region. Plotted O2 is the post-burn sensor reading.
BAS-01's own ISS result. BAS-04 Fig. 4 shows the same point (the team's match) at about 16.1% O2 and about 150 s⁻¹ forced stretch, with the 0.318 cm blowoff marker.
BAS-01 finds its ISS blowoff limits agree well with its 5.18-s drop-tower limits; the highest drop-tower blowoff point of Fig. 6.9 reads about 16.0% final O2 at about 142 s⁻¹.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: A blowoff limit: in BAS-01's ISS tests a cast PMMA rod flame blew off at about 16.1% final O2 as the flow was raised, at stretch about 150 s⁻¹.

answer.not_covered: BAS-01 gives no total pressure, and no flow speed for this limit.

answers.question: What does the burn limit BAS-01:nodate:PMMA-ROD-ISS-BOUNDARY-MINIMUM:df589e15 (PMMA, 13.5% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: The minimum of BAS-01's microgravity flammability boundary for cast PMMA rods in concurrent stagnation flow on the ISS: about 13.5% final O2 at a stretch rate of 8 to 12 s⁻¹ (text value); pressure not reported.

How found: an empirical fit, Eq. 6.1 (final O2 = 6 exp(−0.5a) + 0.0167a + 13.4), joining a quenching and a blowoff branch on Fig. 6.9, which plots final O2 against stretch rate normalised to a 0.318 cm rod radius; fitted range not stated.
The report calls this minimum significantly lower than a cited 1-g upward flame spread limit of 15.4% O2 with an extra 4 cm/s forced flow (Ref. 23; material not stated in the report).
BAS-09 replots this BASS-II boundary (citing BAS-04) with its minimum at about 10 s⁻¹ adjusted stretch rate.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: The lowest point of BAS-01's fitted microgravity boundary for cast PMMA rods in concurrent flow: about 13.5% final O2 at stretch 8 to 12 s⁻¹, from empirical Eq. 6.1.

answer.not_covered: BAS-01 gives no total pressure for these rod tests.

answers.question: What does the burn limit BAS-01:nodate:PMMA-ROD-ISS-LOWEST-FINAL-O2-SUSTAINED:23bb3421 (PMMA, 13.6% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: The lowest final O2 at which flames survived in BAS-01's ISS tests of cast PMMA rods in concurrent stagnation flow, in microgravity: flames ignited at higher O2 survived to 13.6% final O2; stretch rate, rod size and pressure not stated with the value.
How: O2 falls very slowly during a test as products mix into the 250-L glovebox volume; initial and final O2 were read for each test, the readings calibrated against the onboard mass spectrometer.
BAS-01's own result. BAS-04 calls 13.6% the minimum test point of its boundary data, and BAS-09 cites it as the 13.6% minimum needed for stable flames in BASS-II.

Sustained ignition needed more O2: below about 14.5% initial O2 none was obtained; the authors attribute ignition limits lying above flammability limits to the added heat loss into the initially cold rod.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: A surviving-flame limit: in BAS-01's ISS tests, cast PMMA rods lit at higher O2 kept burning in concurrent flow down to 13.6% final O2.

answer.not_covered: BAS-01 gives no total pressure for these rod tests.

answers.question: What does the burn limit BAS-01:nodate:PMMA-ROD-ISS-QUENCH-FIG6.10-LOG-A1.3:7ac5cb01 (PMMA, 16% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: Quenching limit (flame out at low flow) from a BAS-01 ISS test of cast PMMA rods in concurrent flow (microgravity): about 16.0% final O2 at a stretch rate of about 1.3 s⁻¹ (the lowest-stretch quench point, read from Fig. 6.10).

Method: hot-wire ignition at the rod tip, generally at 5 cm/s; the flow was then lowered in steps held at least 100 s each until the flame quenched (tests up to 28 min); plotted O2 is the post-burn reading.
Nearby on Fig. 6.10 an ISS stable flame reads about 15.6% final O2 at about 1.1 s⁻¹, its stretch error bar spanning below 1 to about 3.4 s⁻¹.

BAS-01's own ISS result. Fig. 6.10 replots the Fig. 6.9 data on a log stretch axis, expanding the quenching branch and stressing the flow uncertainty below 1 cm/s; the team read this value from Fig. 6.10 only. Flames along this boundary are sensitive to perturbations that can put them out (cited, Ref. 22).

other_side.note: a stable flame at lower O2 and a lower stretch rate

lead.text: A quenching limit of BAS-01's ISS cast PMMA rods: flame out at about 16.0% final O2, stretch about 1.3 s⁻¹; a nearby stable flame: about 15.6% at about 1.1 s⁻¹.

answer.not_covered: BAS-01 gives no total pressure for these rod tests.

answers.question: What does the burn limit BAS-01:nodate:PMMA-ROD-ISS-QUENCH-FIG6.9-A0-HI1:6afdc210 (PMMA, 18% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: A quenching limit point: in BAS-01's Fig. 6.9, one of the two highest 'ISS quench' points, about 18.0% final O2 at a forced stretch rate of about 0 s⁻¹ (read from a figure), for a cast PMMA rod in concurrent flow, microgravity, ISS glovebox.
To find quenching limits the flow was lowered in steps, each held at least 100 s; each test's extinction flow and last stable flow, with the post-burn O2 reading, define the Fig. 6.9 boundary.

Stretch rate is a = (3/2)(U/r)(r/ro)^½, U the free-stream velocity, normalised to the 0.318-cm base rod radius; the report stresses the flow uncertainty at very low velocities (<1 cm/s) along the quenching branch.
It is BAS-01's own ISS measurement; BAS-04's Fig. 4 shows the same point (the team's match) at about 18.0% final O2 near zero forced stretch, coloured as a 0.318-cm rod.

inferred.text: Set against the boundary minimum, about 13.5% final O2 at a = 8 to 12 s⁻¹, this limit marks the steep rise of the quenching branch towards zero stretch.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: A quenching limit: a cast PMMA rod flame in microgravity on the ISS went out at about 18.0% final O2 near zero stretch, found by lowering the flow stepwise.

answer.not_covered: Neither document gives the flow speed behind this limit.

answers.question: What does the burn limit BAS-01:nodate:PMMA-ROD-ISS-STABLE-FIG6.9-A4:c5d4047f (PMMA, 13.6% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: Stable-flame point (burning side), the last flow with a stable flame in a BAS-01 ISS test of cast PMMA rods in concurrent stagnation flow (microgravity): about 13.6% final O2 at a stretch rate of about 4 s⁻¹ (lowest-O2 ISS stable point, read from Fig. 6.9).

Method: each ISS test gives its extinction flow and its last stable-flame flow; flow was stepped down to quenching (steps held at least 100 s) or raised to blowoff; plotted O2 is the post-burn reading.
BAS-01's own ISS result. Its text separately states that flames ignited at higher O2 survived to final O2 as low as 13.6%, with no stretch rate given for that value.
On Fig. 6.9 the lowest ISS quench point and the two lowest ISS blowoff points read about 13.5% final O2, at stretch rates of about 7 to 8, 15 and 38 s⁻¹.

answers.question: What does the burn limit BAS-01:nodate:PMMA-ROD-ISS-SUSTAINED-IGNITION-LIMIT:577ceb4b (PMMA, 14.5% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: Sustained-ignition limit for cast PMMA rods in BAS-01's ISS tests (microgravity, concurrent flow, ignition generally at 5 cm/s): below about 14.5% initial O2 no sustained flame was obtained, though flames showed while the igniter was on and briefly after.

The astronaut held a hot wire within a millimetre of the rod tip, powered until a stable flame formed, re-powering it if the flame seemed to die; at very low O2, ignition up to 500 s at 2 to 10 cm/s initial flow gave none.
BAS-01's own measurement, on initial O2 calibrated with the onboard mass spectrometer; text: about 14.5%; edge of its Fig. 6.2 'Observed O2 ignition limit' box: about 14.7 to 14.8%.
Flames ignited at higher O2 survived to 13.6% final O2; the authors attribute ignition limits lying above flammability limits to the added heat loss into the initially cold rod.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: A sustained-ignition limit: in BAS-01's ISS tests, cast PMMA rods in concurrent flow gave no lasting flame below about 14.5% initial O2, despite long hot-wire ignition.

answer.not_covered: BAS-01 gives no total pressure for these rod tests.

answers.question: What does the burn limit BAS-01:nodate:REF23-1G-UPWARD-LIMIT:a592501e (Material not stated in the source, 15.4% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: An upward flame spread limit on Earth (normal gravity) of 15.4% O2, with an additional 4 cm/s forced flow, which BAS-01 cites from Hirsch et al. (Ref. 23, ASTM STP1454, 2003).

How BAS-01 places it: Fig. 6.22 puts the point at a flow ratio U/U_D of about 12 (U_D = 2 cm/s), assuming linear superposition of a 20 cm/s buoyant velocity at the flame base (Ref. 32) and the 4 cm/s forced flow.
BAS-01 finds its ISS boundary minimum for cast PMMA rods, about 13.5% final O2 at a forced stretch rate (normalised to a 0.318 cm rod) of 8 to 12 s⁻¹, significantly lower than this 15.4% limit.
In Fig. 6.22 the Hirsch 1-g point falls inside the stochastic BASS-II boundary.

inferred.text: OVR-13 plots 'Hirsch 1g 1 atm' points for PMMA rods at about 15.4% and about 14.5% O2 (read from a slide, its Hirsch source not cited); the 15.4% may be this limit, but no document links the two.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Cited from another study: BAS-01 quotes Hirsch et al.'s upward spread limit on Earth, 15.4% O2 with 4 cm/s added forced flow, beside its ISS rod boundary.

answers.question: Why did test BAS-03:September10,2009:D-08-14:18d915fe (Nomex HT90-40, 19.9% O2) go out?

data.text: Test D-08-14: Nomex HT90-40 fabric at 19.9% and 101.3 kPa (14.7 psia) ended in EXTINCTION. Oxygen and lunar gravity are the team's reading: the card labels neither, nor any flow or igniter.

The team counts this card among the tests behind OVR-04's lunar-gravity MOC* for Nomex HT90-40 at 101.3 kPa, 19.9% O2: the highest O2 at which it went out during the drop, a criterion OVR-04 says differs from 1 g because of drop-time limits.
In the same table, the lunar-gravity ULOI* of this fabric at 101.3 kPa is 21.0% O2, the lowest O2 at which it burned for the full drop time; OVR-04 cites its lunar values from earlier work.
The OVR-04 authors explain that when Nomex fibres are heated they swell and close the spaces between them, which stops air moving through the fabric and so inhibits heat transfer through it.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: In what the team reads as a lunar-gravity test, Nomex HT90-40 fabric went out at 19.9% O2 and 101.3 kPa; the card gives no cause for the extinction.

answer.not_covered: No other lunar-gravity test of this fabric is recorded.

data.text: A 1-cm-wide flat acrylic (PMMA) sample, thickness not stated, burned aboard the ISS in air (about 20.9% O2) at around 9 cm/s, flow direction relative to the flame not stated; it went out in the last two frames of a montage taken 1.3 s apart.

The slide says the 500 cc/min nitrogen flow weakened but did not extinguish the flame; it gives no cause for the extinction that follows 'Nitrogen off'.
The deck's conclusions add that extinction with the nitrogen jet was not possible at the given flow rate; that bullet gives no rate, sample, O2, pressure or air speed.

As the montage images appear (a description, not the slide's words), the flame shrinks up to 'Flame Minimum', then grows with a bright yellow-orange core while nitrogen is still on; the two 'Flame extinguishes' frames show a blue outline.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

answers.question: What does the burn limit BAS-04:nodate:PMMA-ROD-DROP-FIG4-DB-R0.318-A94.5:f6e137d2 (PMMA, 15% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: Blowoff limit from BAS-04's 5.18-s drop-tower tests (microgravity) of a PMMA rod of 0.318 cm radius (6.35 mm diameter): about 15.0% final O2 at a forced stretch rate of about 94.5 s⁻¹, read from Fig. 4.

Method: the rod was lit in normal gravity and burned briefly at a flammable O2 flow to preheat; the gas was then switched to the test atmosphere and the package released as it reached the flame. Plotted O2 is the post-burn reading.

BAS-04's own drop tests, run to compare blowoff in short and long microgravity. The authors find their linear fit (final O2 = 0.0181x + 13.42, x = forced stretch, s⁻¹) agrees very well with the ISS blowoff data (fit 0.02x + 13.3).
Drop-tower blowoff flames were significantly smaller than the ISS flames; the authors attribute this most likely to the short burn before blowoff, which left the rod little preheated.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: A drop-tower blowoff limit: in BAS-04's 5.18-s drop tests in microgravity a 0.318-cm-radius PMMA rod flame blew off at about 15.0% final O2, stretch about 94.5 s⁻¹.

answer.not_covered: BAS-04 prints no pressure, diluent or flow speed for its drop tests.

data.text: Low-speed quenching limit from BAS-05 for 2.2 cm wide, about 0.32 mm SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass) in concurrent flow on the ISS, microgravity, 101.33 kPa: where the experimental boundary crosses 17.2% O2, at about 2.9 cm/s, read from a figure.

answers.question: What does the burn limit BAS-09:nodate:PMMA-ROD-R0.318CM-1G-BLOWOFF-O2-15:d148ef69 (PMMA, 15% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

answers.question: Why did test BAS-09:nodate:PMMA-ROD-ZGRF-WIND-TUNNEL-14PCT-2CMS:0571f899 (PMMA, 14% O2) go out?

data.text: BAS-09 repeated its 14% O2, 2 cm/s normal-gravity case in the ZGRF wind tunnel rig, a 20 cm diameter flow system much less prone to drawing in air from the top: the cast PMMA rod flame blew off (went out) in repeated tests.
The authors' explanation for the quartz tube at 14% O2: at low forced flow, air entering from the tube top might mix with the supplied gas, raising the O2 so the rod remained flammable.
In the 7.6 cm quartz tube at the same 14% O2 and 2 cm/s (normal gravity), the asymmetric cast PMMA rod flame did not blow off.
Given these check runs, BAS-09 discarded its 14% O2 data from further analysis.

other_side.note: the same 14% O2, 2 cm/s case did not blow off in the quartz tube

lead.text: At 14% O2 and 2 cm/s in normal gravity, a PMMA rod flame blew off in the ZGRF tunnel but not the quartz tube, where the authors suspect entrained air.

answer.not_covered: BAS-09 gives no rod radius, flow direction, pressure or run count for the 14% O2 ZGRF tests.

answers.question: Why did test BASS:4 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 21.9% O2) burn?

data.text: A 2 cm wide, 0.32 mm SIBAL strip burned in microgravity in the ISS glovebox at 21.9% O2 and 98.29 kPa in 10 cm/s concurrent flow, pre-wired igniter; the log gives a burn of about 40 s and does not say how the flame ended.

BAS-01 Table 7.1 lists GMT96-T7 (this test, by the team's match) at 21% O2 and 10 cm/s; the report's Fig. 7.2 run at those printed conditions burned to complete burnout in about 40 s, but is not tied to a test number.

In that run the igniter started a flame on both sides, which reached steady spread at about 19 s and held it around 9 s; BAS-01's Fig. 7.4, whose steady spread means a constant rate for more than 20 s, gives about 2.73 mm/s for 2.2 cm in microgravity at 21% O2 and about 10 cm/s (read from a figure).

inferred.text: This test's 21.9% O2 is above the whole oxygen range of the quenching boundary BAS-05 draws for 2.2 cm SIBAL in concurrent flow, about 16.8 to 18.9% O2 at about 2.2 to 3.7 cm/s (read from a figure), and its 10 cm/s flow is above those speeds.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: BASS:4 (2 cm SIBAL, microgravity, 21.9% O2, 10 cm/s concurrent flow) burned for about 40 s; the log does not say how the flame ended.

answer.not_covered: No spread rate is tied to this test by its number.

In the thesis's ISS burner tests, nominal oxygen of 26% and above can in general give steady flames, thin and blue, that grow slowly over minutes (pressure not stated for this statement).
Test BRE:20339A0, same burner, still air, microgravity, went out at 37.52% O2 and 105.5 kPa; the thesis lists it as both an ethylene-nitrogen and a methane-nitrogen test (fuel not settled).

The author separates steady from self-extinguished flames by a computed flame temperature of 1100–1200 K (1100 K alone in Chapter 4), fuel-terminated flames lying above it; the thesis's Fig. 5.2 also shows some fuel-terminated flames computed below that band and some self-extinguished ones above it.

inferred.text: Tests on this burner at nearly the same oxygen and pressure ended both ways, so oxygen and pressure alone do not settle the outcome here; the thesis reports that lower fuel heats of combustion and higher oxygen help flames burn longer (round 1).

For the 50 mm ethylene-nitrogen tests of Table F.1, the author's model estimated flame temperatures (radiative-fraction correlation, Eq. 6.17) to judge whether the flames could reach steady state; all fell below the 1100–1200 K critical range.

The thesis's Chapter 6 summary, covering 146 ISS flames on the 25 mm burner, states that every flame ignited at nominal 25% or 21% O2 self-extinguished within 90 s (ethylene or ethylene-nitrogen fuel, microgravity).

inferred.text: In Table F.1 every test below 33% O2, this one included, self-extinguished; the lowest-oxygen test that burned to fuel shut-off is BRE:20247F1 at 33% O2, 108 kPa (all in quiescent air).

lead.text: BRE:21028G4 (50 mm burner, ISS microgravity, quiescent air, 24% O2, 105 kPa) self-extinguished; the author's model put every 50 mm flame below the 1100–1200 K critical range for steady burning.

answers.question: Why did test CAB-03:nodate:CREW-CLOTHING-FABRIC-37:a865f471 (blend of para-aramid, meta-aramid and antistatic fibers (crew clothing fabric), 37% O2) go out?

data.text: A commercial blend of para-aramid, meta-aramid and antistatic fibers, the crew clothing fabric, passed NASA-STD-6001B Test 1 on its own at 37% O2 and 56.5 kPa (8.2 psia), in 1 g on the ground by the team's reading.

Citing the standard, CAB-03 says Test 1 lights a vertical specimen at its bottom with a chemical igniter for about 25–30 s in a closed 1400-liter chamber; the material passes if none of five specimens burns over 6 in or spreads flame by burning debris.

With a meta-aramid tape / brass-teeth zipper sewn with commercial PTFE thread, the same fabric also passed flammability testing at 37% O2 and 56.5 kPa (8.2 psia); CAB-03 reports no result for its other seam and zipper configurations.

CAB-03 says textiles that pass on their own may still fail in a configuration with other textiles. It concludes that the combined performance of components such as zipper, thread and hook and loop, not only the outermost layer, must be fire-resistant.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: The para-aramid, meta-aramid and antistatic crew clothing fabric passed 1-g Test 1 (team's reading) on its own at 37% O2 and 56.5 kPa; CAB-03 gives no mechanism for the pass.

answer.not_covered: CAB-03 prints no burn length or MOC for this fabric, only the pass at 37% O2.

data.text: A PTFE woven fabric layered with a blue cotton fabric failed NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 (upward flame, chemical igniter at the bottom) at 32% O2, in 1 g by the team's reading; pressure not printed for this panel.
CAB-03 notes that the PTFE fabric is less flammable than cotton, its layup partner. It also says textiles that pass on their own may still fail in a configuration with other textiles.
Tested on its own, the same PTFE woven fabric passed Test 1 at 36% O2 and 56.5 kPa, 1 g by the team's reading, with a char length under 6 in and no drip or melt.
The same layup also failed at 36% O2 and 56.5 kPa (8.2 psia), where both fabrics burned through, and at 34% O2 (pressure not printed).

inferred.text: In Fig. 1 the PTFE fabric passed alone at 36% O2 and 56.5 kPa, while the layup with cotton failed at 32% O2 (pressure not printed), 4 points lower; CAB-03 gives no MOC for either, so the full shift is not known.

answers.question: Why did test FLARE:RUN#01 (Filter paper, 14.3% O2) go out?

data.text: 0.12 mm filter paper, 40 mm wide, microgravity (ISS/Kibo SCEM), 100 kPa, 14.3% O2 and 6 cm/s opposed flow, Kanthal hot wire on from T + 5 s for 10 s: the flame went out immediately after ignition.

The pre-flight model expected a minimum limiting oxygen of 14.0% at 8 cm/s opposed flow and a much wider flammable range below 10 cm/s; the authors write that, contrary to these predictions, this run's flame went out immediately.

Below 10 cm/s opposed flow the measured limiting oxygen was higher than the pre-flight curve; the authors attribute this to the sample's boundary layer, where preheat length varies inversely with the square root of opposed flow.

inferred.text: This run's 14.3% O2 at 6 cm/s lies below the updated model's predicted limiting oxygen of 15.8% at 5 cm/s and 14.8% at 8 cm/s opposed flow, which would put it on the non-burning side of the revised curve.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Run #01 went out right after ignition at 14.3% O2 and 6 cm/s opposed flow in microgravity, which the authors note was contrary to their pre-flight prediction.

answer.not_covered: No repeat of this run's 14.3% O2, 6 cm/s condition in the documents.

answers.question: What does the burn limit FLR-05:nodate:ETFE-CU#2-1G-HOI:68220648 (ETFE wire insulation, 44.2% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: ETFE–Cu#2 wire's 1-g high gas velocity oxygen index (HOI, ISO 4589-4): the limiting oxygen concentration for downward spread against 80 cm/s upward forced flow, about 44.2% O2 in O2/N2, read from FLR-05 Fig. 7c; pressure not reported.

FLR-05 lit the insulation by gas torch at under 10 cm/s (HOI speeds: hot-wire anemometer values), set the test flow once the flame passed 35 mm down, and counted spread past a line 60 mm from the holder bottom as flammable, in up-and-down O2 steps.

FLR-05's own ground measurement. Its 1-g series for this wire, read from Fig. 7c: OI about 35.7% O2 (run at 4 cm/s, plotted at 35 cm/s), HOI about 39.8, 42.1, 44.2 and 46.7% at 40, 60, 80 and 100 cm/s opposed flow (the 100 cm/s reading low confidence).

The authors recommend the HOI at 60–100 cm/s for predicting the minimum LOC (MLOC): with forced flow far above natural convection the experimenter controls the effective velocity at extinction, while flame-induced natural convection dominates at small forced flow.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: ETFE–Cu#2 wire's HOI on Earth at 80 cm/s opposed flow, about 44.2% O2: the limiting oxygen concentration FLR-05 found in ISO 4589-4 up-and-down runs, read from Fig. 7c.

answer.not_covered: FLR-05 does not report the pressure or the number of runs behind its ground limits.

FLR-05 lit the insulation by gas torch at under 10 cm/s (HOI speeds: hot-wire anemometer values), set the test flow once the flame passed 35 mm down, and counted spread past a line 60 mm from the holder bottom as flammable, in up-and-down O2 steps.

FLR-05's own ground measurement. Its 1-g series for this wire, read from Fig. 7d: OI about 35.85% O2 (run at 4 cm/s, plotted at 35 cm/s), HOI about 42.4, 43.9, 47.7 and 51.4% at 40, 60, 80 and 100 cm/s opposed flow (the 100 cm/s reading low confidence).

The authors recommend the HOI at 60–100 cm/s for predicting the minimum LOC (MLOC): with forced flow far above natural convection the experimenter controls the effective velocity at extinction, while flame-induced natural convection dominates at small forced flow.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: ETFE–NiCr#2 wire's HOI on Earth at 80 cm/s opposed flow, about 47.7% O2: the limiting oxygen concentration FLR-05 found in ISO 4589-4 up-and-down runs, read from Fig. 7d.

answer.not_covered: FLR-05 does not report the pressure or the number of runs behind its ground limits.

answers.question: Why did test OVR-03:nodate:KIMWIPES-FIG9-CON30:227dd5be (Kimwipes tissue paper, 40% O2) burn?

data.text: Kimwipes tissue (thin cellulose), 5 × 10 cm, microgravity drop-tower rig, about 40% O2 in a normoxic atmosphere, 30 cm/s concurrent flow, hot wire lit at release: burned, spreading at about 26 mm/s (read from a figure).

The authors tested Kimwipes, thin cellulose that chars as it burns and is not treated for fire resistance, to expand the thin-cellulose database; with it they can obtain spread and extinction data in the short drop time.
Along the normoxic curve, the report's correlations predict opposed spread rising quickly with O2 and concurrent spread rising more slowly, as the falling pressure offsets the rising O2.
In this Fig. 9 series (microgravity, 30 cm/s concurrent flow), spread went from about 22 mm/s at about 24% O2 to about 31 mm/s at about 85% (read from the figure).

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

Each 5 × 10 cm sample was lit by a hot wire in 1 g in enriched oxygen; the test gas reached it shortly after the 5.18 s drop began, leaving the flame about 5 s in it.

answers.question: What does the burn limit OVR-03:nodate:VITONA-1G-MOC:69d467ab (Viton A, 21% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: Earth-gravity maximum oxygen concentration (1g MOC) of Viton A in the upward NASA-STD-6001 Test 1 at about 101.35 kPa: about 21% O2, read from the report's Fig. 10, which plots 1g MOC against total pressure.

The report defines the 1g MOC, citing the Test 1 standard, as the oxygen at which at least five samples passed, with at least one failure at 1% more O2. Fig. 10 plots cited WSTF data (its ref. 7), without sample form, thickness or igniter.
In the same Fig. 10 series, Viton A's 1g MOC reads about 21% O2 at about 85.5 kPa and about 29% at about 48.26 kPa.

The report says most Test 1 MOCs vary mainly with oxygen, not pressure, and the few exceptions appear to share halogens (the legend marks Viton A as containing them); it attributes this to halogens scavenging free radicals, which inhibits the flame's heat release; at low pressure more diffusive mixing increases scavenging, and the reduced heat release raises the oxygen limit.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Viton A's Earth-gravity Test 1 MOC, the highest oxygen at which samples consistently self-extinguish, at about 101.35 kPa: about 21% O2, cited WSTF data read from the report's Fig. 10.

answer.not_covered: No microgravity or partial-gravity test of Viton A in the documents.

Table I lists 18.0% O2 at 70.3 kPa as this film's Martian-gravity ULOI*, the lowest oxygen at which a flame survived the full drop time; the paper describes this test as burning at that condition.
When the oxygen was lowered to 17% in another Martian-gravity test, the Mylar flame went out (pressure not printed for that test).

The authors link Mylar's significantly negative oxygen margin in Martian, Lunar and 0g to the absence of gravity-induced dripping, which keeps heated molten fuel in the flame zone, as in metals combustion.

The Ferkul et al. 2026 presentation's authors state that numerical and experimental evidence suggests Lunar gravity is nearly the most flammable condition.

In BAS-07's normal-gravity test of SIBAL fabric in normal air, the flame did not propagate downward: it broke up and went out; the deck says downward spread over this material is not possible in normal air.
A linear fit printed for Test 2-29's flame-base position reads Vf = 0.86t + 35.2 (position in mm, t in s), R² = 0.9969.

other_side.note: in normal gravity a downward SIBAL flame went out

lead.text: In a Lunar-gravity aircraft test at 21% O2 and 101.3 kPa, 5 cm SIBAL burned downward for all 20 s; in normal-gravity air, a downward SIBAL flame went out.

answer.not_covered: The slides print no ignition method, sample length or airflow speed for Test 2-29.

answers.question: Why did test SAF-04:nodate:1-1-1G:a69a4a40 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), % O2) burn?

data.text: SAF-04 Table I prints, beside flight sample 1-1, a normal-gravity (1-g) result for the same 0.37 mm SIBAL fabric: burn length 'Complete' and spread rate 'Acceleratory'.

Citing its Ref. 1, SAF-02 notes that upward spread is usually acceleratory in 1 g, and that 1-g ground tests with SIBAL cloth spread steadily when flame size was limited by heat loss or lower pressure.
In the same table, the 1-g columns of the opposed-flow row 1-2 give a burn length of about 0 and a spread rate of n/a.

In microgravity, flight test 1-1 (20 cm/s concurrent, 21.7% O2 initial, near 22.6 on SAF-04's chart) spread 1.8 mm/s over about 84 cm before the flow was shut off at 420 s; SAF-04 concludes that, unlike in 1-g, a steady flame was achieved even on a wide sample in concurrent flow.

inferred.text: Table I's 1-g 'Acceleratory' spread for this fabric contrasts with the steady spread of its microgravity flight samples, the contrast SAF-02 and SAF-04 describe between 1-g upward and low-gravity spread; the 1-g conditions are not printed.

other_side.note: Table I's 1-g column of opposed-flow row 1-2: burn length about 0

lead.text: In 1-g, conditions unprinted, SAF-04 Table I records this SIBAL fabric burning completely with acceleratory spread, but about 0 burn length in its opposed-flow row; no cause stated.

answer.not_covered: SAF-04 prints no oxygen, pressure, flow or sample size for its 1-g tests.

answers.question: Why did test SAF-04:nodate:2-1-1G:9f028457 (Silicone (MQ), % O2) burn?

data.text: SAF-04 Table I prints, beside flight sample 2-1, a normal-gravity (1-g) result for the same 0.27 mm silicone burning upward: burn length '~ Complete', spread 'Acceleratory'; the slides say such samples were almost always completely consumed.

The SAF-04 authors suggest, perhaps, that 1-g's larger buoyant flow could sweep out the silica powder that may deposit on the fuel and impede pyrolysis, and might aid the cracking and flaking that exposes fresh fuel.

In microgravity, flight sample 2-1 of the same thickness, burning upward in 20 cm/s concurrent flow at 22.1% O2 initial (about 21.5% on SAF-04's chart), did not spread, which the authors found surprising.

sources.locator: Saffire-2 Measured Oxygen chart, top panel (samples 1 to 6)

data.text: SAF-04 says its upward 1-g tests spanned the flammability limits by thickness: 0.27 mm samples almost always completely consumed, 0.61 mm burning on average 7.6 of the available 30 cm before going out, 1.03 mm not burning at all.

other_side.note: flight sample 2-1 of the same thickness did not spread in microgravity

lead.text: In upward Earth tests, 0.27 mm silicone sheets almost always burned completely, but in orbit the same thickness did not spread; authors suggest buoyant flow may clear silica powder.

answer.not_covered: SAF-04 prints no oxygen, pressure, flow or test count for its 1-g silicone tests.

answers.question: Why did test SAF-04:nodate:2-8-1G:7f51c48f (PMMA, % O2) burn?

data.text: SAF-04 Table I prints, beside flight sample 2-8 (a PMMA slab of nominal 1 cm thickness), a normal-gravity (1-g) result: burn length 'Complete', spread rate 'Acceleratory'.

The SAF-08 authors describe PMMA in 1 g: air mixes in from more than one side, so the pyrolysis gas always finds enough oxidant and the flame burns vigorously, its pyrolysis area moving quickly up the sample.

In microgravity, flight sample 2-8 burned 600 s in 20 cm/s concurrent flow, its flame anchored at the sample base; Table I's burn length, about 10 cm, is the fuel length with significant visible damage.
SAF-09 notes that upward flame spread is usually acceleratory in normal gravity (its refs. 43 and 44).

other_side.note: no 1-g test of this PMMA slab that went out in the documents

lead.text: In Earth tests this PMMA slab burned completely with accelerating spread; the SAF-08 authors describe air mixing in from several sides in upward burning on Earth, feeding a vigorous flame.

answer.not_covered: SAF-04 prints no oxygen, pressure, flow, burning direction or test count for its 1-g PMMA tests.

answers.question: Why did test SAF-09:nodate:PMMA:3bcce38b (PMMA, 20.9% O2) burn?

data.text: In a 1-g pressure-chamber tunnel, a 10 mm cast PMMA slab in air at 80 ±2 kPa with 20 cm/s upward (concurrent) forced flow spread to the sample end at about 0.69 mm/s (pyrolysis front, read from a figure; 3–5 replicates).

The SAF-09 authors state their tests lie away from the limits where flame chemistry may matter (low oxygen, low pressure, blowoff at large flow, very low flow in microgravity), so spread primarily follows flame-to-solid heat transfer.

SAF-09 finds Saffire II sample 9's microgravity rate (atmospheric pressure, 20 cm/s concurrent) significantly lower than the 1-g rate at that pressure; the authors infer an important role of buoyancy-induced flow in 1-g concurrent spread.
From the flame tip the same figure reads about 0.77 mm/s at 80 kPa; SAF-09 puts more confidence in the pyrolysis-front values because of the flame-tip error.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: In Earth tests at 80 kPa in air, 10 mm PMMA burned to the sample end; SAF-09's authors place these tests away from limits where flame chemistry may matter.

answer.not_covered: SAF-09 tested only air at one flow speed.

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-III:III-1 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 21% O2) burn?

data.text: In microgravity aboard Cygnus, a 94 cm long SIBAL fabric burned in 25 cm/s concurrent flow (30 cm/s in the PSI-100 record) at 21% O2 and 100 kPa in SAF-02 (SAF-06: 21.2%, 99 kPa, spreading 2.3 mm/s); SAF-02 and SAF-06 report it from earlier papers.

SAF-02 reports that all Saffire I–V cotton and SIBAL samples settled to a steady spread rate and flame size, the rate depending on oxygen and flow; its Table 2 gives this test a steady size of 5 cm after a maximum of 8.2 cm.
Citing its Ref. 1, SAF-02 reports a flame-size overshoot in Saffire I and III and attributes it to boundary-layer development on the sample surface.

SAF-06 concludes the overshoot cannot come only from the flame moving into a growing boundary layer on the sample, because the Saffire V cotton, which burns away and leaves no boundary layer upstream of its base, also overshot.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: In microgravity, SIBAL test III-1 burned in 25 cm/s concurrent flow (PSI record: 30 cm/s), settling to a steady 5 cm flame; no document gives a specific cause.

answer.not_covered: No igniter details are given for this test.

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-II:2-1 (Silicone (MQ), 22.1% O2) go out?

data.text: In microgravity on an ISS resupply vehicle, a 0.27 mm silicone sheet burning upward in 20 cm/s concurrent flow at 22.1% O2 initial (ISS reading; about 21.5% on SAF-04's chart) did not spread; burn length about 0.

sources.locator: Saffire-2 Measured Oxygen chart, top panel (samples 1 to 6)

data.text: The authors call silicone's microgravity behaviour perplexing, perhaps due to its complex burning: its fine silica powder could deposit on the fuel and impede pyrolysis, while 1-g's larger buoyant flow could sweep it out.

In normal-gravity upward tests (oxygen, pressure and flow not printed), 0.27 mm silicone samples were almost always completely consumed; SAF-04 calls it surprising that not even this thin sample permitted any flame spread in microgravity.
After the 80 W, 9.2 s igniter was powered off, a tiny gas-phase flame remained but did not spread and quickly went out; SAF-04 says the igniters appeared to work normally.

other_side.note: 0.27 mm sheets almost always burned completely in upward 1-g tests

lead.text: In orbit, this 0.27 mm silicone sheet's flame died without spreading, though such sheets almost always burned up in upward Earth tests; the authors suggest silica powder may hinder burning.

answer.not_covered: No microgravity silicone test at a flow other than 20 cm/s.

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-II:2-5 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 22.1% O2) burn?

data.text: In microgravity on an ISS resupply vehicle, a 5 cm wide, 0.37 mm SIBAL fabric burned its whole length in 20 cm/s concurrent flow at about 22.1% O2 (SAF-04 chart: about 21.5%; SAF-02: 21%, 100 kPa; SAF-06: 22.1%, 103 kPa), spreading 2.1 mm/s.

At the same 20 cm/s concurrent flow it spread marginally faster than wide test 1-1, 2.1 against 1.8 mm/s; the SAF-04 authors attribute this partly to the slightly higher starting oxygen, 22.1% against 21.7%, and add that side entrainment might contribute.
SAF-04 Table I gives this row's normal-gravity (1-g) result as burn length 'Complete' with acceleratory spread; the 1-g oxygen, pressure, flow and sample size are not printed.

SAF-04 reports that earlier experience with cellulosic fuels had suggested a material whose flame persists in upward 1-g tests would also burn in microgravity at a moderate flow speed below typical buoyant flow speeds.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: In microgravity, SIBAL test 2-5 burned its whole length in 20 cm/s concurrent flow, and completely in 1-g; SAF-04 attributes its faster spread than 1-1 partly to higher starting oxygen.

answer.not_covered: SAF-04 prints no pressure for the Saffire II tests.

data.text: In microgravity on an ISS resupply vehicle, a 5 cm wide, 0.37 mm SIBAL fabric burned its whole length in 25 cm/s concurrent flow at about 22.1% O2 (SAF-04 chart: about 21.5%; SAF-02: 21%, 100 kPa; SAF-06: 22.1%, 103 kPa), spreading 2.6 mm/s.

SAF-04 Table I gives this row's normal-gravity (1-g) result as burn length 'Complete' with acceleratory spread; the 1-g oxygen, pressure, flow and sample size are not printed.

SAF-04 reports that earlier experience with cellulosic fuels had suggested a material whose flame persists in upward 1-g tests would also burn in microgravity at a moderate flow speed below typical buoyant flow speeds.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-II:2-7 (PMMA & Nomex, 22.1% O2) not ignite?

data.text: In microgravity on an unoccupied ISS resupply vehicle, in 20 cm/s concurrent flow at 22.1% O2 initial (SAF-04 chart: about 21.5%), a 5 cm wide thin PMMA sheet burned away over its 5 cm, but the Nomex HT 90-40 fabric beyond it did not ignite.

SAF-04 reports the PMMA took about two minutes to burn away (Table I: 140 s), its flame plume heating the base of the Nomex all the while; despite this significant heating load the fabric did not ignite.
SAF-04 states that on Earth Nomex HT90-40 burns only if the oxygen concentration is raised to around 24 to 25%; test method, pressure, sample size and source are not printed.
SAF-04 estimates the average flame power of the PMMA at 460 ± 50 W, a calculation assuming complete conversion of the fuel.

inferred.text: At 22.1% O2 initial (about 21.5% on SAF-04's chart) this test ran below the around 24 to 25% that SAF-04 gives for Nomex HT90-40 to burn on Earth, so its non-ignition here does not show how the fabric behaves in microgravity at higher oxygen.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: In microgravity at about 21.5–22.1% O2 and 20 cm/s concurrent flow, test 2-7's Nomex HT90-40 did not ignite though the burning PMMA heated its base for 140 s.

answer.not_covered: SAF-04 prints no pressure for the Saffire II tests.

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-II:2-8 (PMMA, % O2) burn?

data.text: In microgravity on an ISS resupply vehicle, a PMMA slab nominally 1 cm thick, 0.4 cm in its grooved middle 1.8 cm, burned 600 s in 20 cm/s concurrent flow at 22.1 to 22.0% O2 (Table I; about 21.5% on SAF-04's chart).

sources.locator: Saffire-2 Measured Oxygen chart, bottom panel (samples 7 to 9)

data.text: Table I footnote iv: the flames stayed anchored at the sample base, which regressed very slowly, 0.01 to 0.04 mm/s; the about 10 cm burn length is the fuel length with significant visible damage.
The SAF-08 authors argue that in microgravity with forced flow only the base of a PMMA flame is well supplied with oxygen, so the burning zone cannot travel over the surface.
SAF-04 states that samples 2-8 and 2-9 had slightly more powerful igniters, 97 W instead of 80 W, left on longer, 30 s instead of 9.2 s, to assure ignition of these thick fuels.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: In orbit this thick PMMA slab, lit by a stronger igniter left on longer, kept a flame anchored at its base; SAF-08's authors argue only the base gets enough oxygen.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no spread rate or pressure for this grooved sample.

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-IV:IV-1 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 22% O2) burn?

data.text: In microgravity aboard Cygnus, a 50 cm long SIBAL fabric burned in 20 cm/s flow, concurrent in SAF-01 and SAF-02 (opposed in SAF-03's caption), at 22.0% O2 and 100.0 kPa (SAF-03: 23%, 98.0 kPa; SAF-06: 23.1%, 99 kPa), spreading 3.6 mm/s (SAF-03, SAF-06).

SAF-02 reports a spread rate about 100% higher than in Saffire I and III (20 and 25 cm/s, 21% O2, 100 kPa, taller duct) and attributes the larger steady flame of Saffire IV, against Saffire I–III, to its reduced duct height.

SAF-06's core-flow estimate, a model, gives more flow acceleration and faster spread in the smaller Saffire IV duct than in Saffire I's, and the authors conclude that duct size affects the flame more than flame size does.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: In microgravity, SIBAL test IV-1 burned in 20 cm/s flow; SAF-02 attributes its larger steady flame than Saffire I–III's to the lower duct.

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-IV:IV-2 (PMMA, 22% O2) burn?

data.text: In microgravity aboard Cygnus, a two-sided 10 mm PMMA slab, preheated 10 min and ignited for 60 s, burned in 20 cm/s flow (concurrent in SAF-02, opposed in SAF-03's caption) at 22.0% O2 and 100.0 kPa; its flame length grew 0.22 mm/s.

SAF-02 reports the flame did not spread appreciably: it stayed fixed at the leading edge and advanced only by surface regression, which SAF-02 calls typical of thick fuels in low gravity and unlike normal gravity.

After 65 s of flow reduced to 5 cm/s the flow was switched off; the PMMA kept bubbling and the flame survived 15 s without flow, then grew extensively. SAF-02 attributes the bubbling to heat built up during the long burn and the survival to mixing by fuel jets leaving the surface.

SAF-02 reports the flame length reached an upper limit, 9.5 cm after 400 s; SAF-03 reports the two-sided samples still growing at the end of the test (around 500 s), with a maximum flame length of 90.8 mm.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: In microgravity, two-sided 10 mm PMMA IV-2 burned at 22.0% O2 in 20 cm/s flow, anchored at the leading edge; SAF-02 calls this typical of thick fuels in low gravity.

answer.not_covered: Neither SAF-02 nor SAF-03 says how this flame finally ended.

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-I:1-1 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 21.7% O2) go out?

data.text: In microgravity on an unoccupied ISS resupply vehicle, a 94 cm long, 0.37 mm SIBAL fabric burned in 20 cm/s concurrent flow at 21.7% O2 initially (ISS reading; SAF-04 chart: near 22.6; SAF-02: 21%, 100 kPa; SAF-06: 21.7%, 102 kPa).

SAF-04 reports the flame burned the whole allotted test time (420 s), spreading 1.8 mm/s in the 20 cm/s concurrent flow over about 84 cm, and went out immediately when the air flow was shut off; about 90% of the fuel burned.

SAF-02 concludes from a Saffire V cotton jersey burn in orbit (26.2% O2, 70.7 kPa; SAF-03: 28%, 74.1 kPa; SAF-06: 26.9%, 76 kPa) that flames on thinner materials can persist for an extended time without forced air flow.

SAF-04's spread-rate summary for this fabric in microgravity marks a 'Quench' line on the concurrent side near zero flow, read at about 2 cm/s; oxygen, pressure and platform of its 1 cm and 2 cm wide series are not printed.

inferred.text: With the flow shut off, test 1-1 sat below the about 2 cm/s concurrent 'Quench' line of SAF-04's summary for this fabric, which fits its immediate extinction; that line is drawn beside the 2 cm wide series, whose oxygen and pressure are not printed.

other_side.note: SAF-02: flames on thinner materials can persist without forced flow (Saffire V cotton jersey)

lead.text: In microgravity, SIBAL test 1-1 went out immediately when the 20 cm/s flow was shut off after 420 s; SAF-02 notes flames on thinner materials can persist without forced flow.

SAF-04 gives this opposed flame a 24 mm length, a bit shorter than the around 40 mm plateau of the concurrent flame of test 1-1 (20 cm/s); how it ended is not stated.
SAF-04 Table I's normal-gravity (1-g) columns give this row a burn length of about 0 and a spread rate of n/a; the oxygen, pressure, flow and set-up of those 1-g tests are not printed.

SAF-04's authors state that on Earth an upward (concurrent-flow) flame is nearly always more hazardous than a downward (opposed-flow) one, while in reduced gravity which is more hazardous depends on flow speed.

inferred.text: For this fabric the opposed-flow flame kept spreading in microgravity at 20 cm/s while Table I's 1-g column beside it shows about no burn; with the 1-g conditions unprinted, the two cannot be compared at equal oxygen or flow.

other_side.note: Table I's 1-g column for this row: burn length about 0

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-VI:VI-3 (PMMA, 30.3% O2) burn?

data.text: In microgravity aboard Cygnus, a two-sided 10 mm PMMA slab burned in 20 cm/s flow (concurrent in SAF-01, opposed in SAF-03's caption) at 30.3% O2 and 54.6 kPa (SAF-03: 30%, 54.4 kPa); its flame length grew 0.38 mm/s in SAF-03.

SAF-03 reports that from two-sided IV-2 (1000 mbar, 0.22 mol fraction O2) to this test (544 mbar, 0.30), both 20 cm/s, the growth rate rose 73% for the 0.08 rise in oxygen despite a 45% drop in total pressure.

SAF-01 reports the flame grew continuously until the flow was reduced to 5 cm/s; SAF-03 then stopped tracking it, the flame having weakened greatly, the low-flow interval being meant to cool the sample so it went out when the flow stopped.

Peak heat release was 3240 W in SAF-03 Table 1 and 3080 W by oxygen-consumption calorimetry in SAF-01 Table 2, over a 780 s burn in SAF-01; SAF-03 calls a peak of 3 kW substantial for a small spacecraft.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: In microgravity, two-sided 10 mm PMMA VI-3 burned in 20 cm/s flow at 30.3% O2 and 54.6 kPa (SAF-01), growing until the flow was reduced; no document states a cause.

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-VI:VI-4 (PMMA, 28.8% O2) burn?

data.text: In microgravity aboard Cygnus, a one-sided 5 mm PMMA slab burned in 20 cm/s flow (concurrent in SAF-01, opposed in SAF-03's caption) at 28.8% O2 and 55.2 kPa (SAF-03: 29%, 55.0 kPa); its flame length grew 0.27 mm/s in SAF-03.

SAF-03 states that its Saffire VI growth rates, 0.27 mm/s here against 0.38 mm/s for two-sided VI-3 (0.30 mol fraction O2 and 544 mbar, against 0.29 and 550 mbar here, both 20 cm/s), show back-side heat loss had a significant effect on growth rate.

SAF-01 reports VI-4 grew continuously until the flow speed was reduced; SAF-03 reports the one-sided samples began to plateau around 380 s (Saffire V) and 420 s (Saffire VI), no time zero given, and offers enhanced back-side heat loss as a plausible cause.
SAF-03 reports the one-sided growth rate did not change from V-3 (0.26 mol fraction O2, 745 mbar) to VI-4 (0.29, 550 mbar), both 20 cm/s, for an oxygen rise of 0.03 mol fraction with a pressure drop.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: In microgravity, one-sided 5 mm PMMA VI-4 burned in 20 cm/s flow, its flame growing 0.27 mm/s; SAF-03 reads its slower growth than two-sided VI-3 as a back-side heat-loss effect.

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-V:V-2 (Cotton fabric, 26.2% O2) burn?

data.text: In microgravity aboard Cygnus, a 50 cm long cotton jersey burned in 20 cm/s concurrent flow (SAF-03's caption: opposed) at 26.2% O2 and 70.7 kPa in SAF-01 and SAF-02; SAF-03 (28%, 74.1 kPa) and SAF-06 (26.9%, 76 kPa) give its spread as 3.4 mm/s.
With the fan off for 70 s from about 280 s, the flame was not put out: it grew back when the flow returned and burned another 150 s until the material was consumed (times as printed in SAF-02).
SAF-02 cannot tell whether surviving blue flamelets or glowing char embers carried the flame through the no-flow period, but judges a surviving flamelet the likely cause of reignition.

SAF-06 finds its spread rate close to that of the Saffire IV SIBAL, 0.34 against 0.36 cm/s at 20 cm/s concurrent, although the atmospheres differed (26.9% O2, 76 kPa against 23.1%, 99 kPa), and says the ratio matches oxygen times the square root of pressure.

inferred.text: SIBAL test 1-1 (20 cm/s concurrent, 21.7% O2 initial, near 22.6 on SAF-04's chart) went out immediately when its flow was shut off, while this cotton survived 70 s without flow at higher oxygen and lower pressure; SAF-02's summary names thin charring fuels at raised oxygen as fuels that cannot be assumed to go out quickly in quiescent conditions.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: In microgravity, cotton jersey test V-2 burned in 20 cm/s flow until consumed, surviving 70 s with the fan off; SAF-02 judges a surviving flamelet the likely cause of reignition.

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-V:V-3 (PMMA, 25.4% O2) go out?

data.text: In microgravity aboard Cygnus, a one-sided 5 mm PMMA slab burned in 20 cm/s flow (concurrent in SAF-02, opposed in SAF-03's caption) at 25.4% O2 and 71.3 kPa (SAF-03: 26%, 74.5 kPa; flame length growth 0.26 mm/s).

After 300 s at 5 cm/s the flame went out at once when the fan was turned off; SAF-02 states the low-flow period cooled the sample better than the quiescent conditions of Saffire IV while keeping fuel vapour from gathering near the surface.
Two-sided 10 mm PMMA test IV-2 (22.0% O2, 100.0 kPa, 20 cm/s, concurrent in SAF-02, opposed in SAF-03's caption) instead survived 15 s without flow after 65 s of reduced flow, then grew extensively.

During the later opposed-flow test V-4 (20 cm/s; 25.7% O2, 72.6 kPa in SAF-02; 26.9%, 76.1 kPa at the start in SAF-08), a flame lit by the upstream flame established briefly on this warm sample, 4.5 cm downstream, then went out; SAF-02 attributes this to the upstream flames growing large enough to consume the available oxygen.

other_side.note: IV-2 survived a flow stop after a shorter low-flow interval

lead.text: In microgravity, one-sided PMMA V-3 went out at once when the flow stopped after 300 s at 5 cm/s; two-sided IV-2 survived a stop after 65 s at reduced flow.

answers.question: Why did test SAFFIRE-V:V-4 (PMMA, 26.9% O2) go out?

data.text: In microgravity aboard Cygnus, a 10 mm cast PMMA slab with 3 mm high ribs 1 to 10 mm wide burned in 20 cm/s opposed flow at 26.9% O2 and 76.1 kPa at the start (SAF-08; SAF-02: 25.7%, 72.6 kPa).

answers.question: What does the burn limit SOF-02:nodate:PMMA-FUNDAMENTALLIMIT:d2cfdf4b (PMMA, 14% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: The lowest O2 that sustains burning, called the fundamental limit after an earlier study: slightly below 14% O2, at the bottom of SOF-02's extinction boundary around 10 cm/s forced flow (strain rate 7.5 1/s); 4-cm PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity, 101.3 kPa (1 ± 0.05 atm).

It rests on SOF-02's 35-test map: O2 and flow read at the duct entrance at extinction (±0.25%), the intermediate-flow boundary found by O2 depletion. Open 'in-between' symbols lie at the extinction boundary's bottom: near 10 cm/s quenching was difficult to tell from blowoff on video.

This is SOF-02's own data. It says this and earlier rod data show the PMMA O2 limit can be below 14%, and calls that considerably lower than the normal-gravity PMMA LOI and upward-flammability values in conventional flammability tables.

The lowest in-between point reads about 13.55% O2 at about 11.5 cm/s. Fig. 8's lowest O2, about 13.3% at about 42.4 cm/s, is a total (wake) blowoff, whose limiting O2 SOF-02 finds lower than for stagnation blowoff.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: The fundamental limit: the lowest O2 sustaining burning of a 4-cm PMMA sphere in ISS microgravity at 101.3 kPa, slightly below 14% around 10 cm/s, from SOF-02's 35-test map.

answer.not_covered: No SoFIE-GEL extinction limit below about 101 kPa is in the documents.

answers.question: What does the burn limit SOF-02:nodate:PMMA-IN-BETWEEN:3c04b989 (PMMA, 14.6% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: An 'in-between' extinction point of SOF-02's own Fig. 8 map, test not named: the O2 recorded at extinction, about 14.6%, at about 9.2 cm/s upstream forced flow (both read from the figure); 4-cm PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity, 101.3 kPa (1 ± 0.05 atm).

Near 10 cm/s quenching was difficult to tell from blowoff on video, so SOF-02 plots some such points as open 'in-between' symbols. At intermediate flows it found the boundary by O2 depletion, O2 and flow read at the duct entrance at the extinction instant (±0.25%).

SOF-02 places the in-between points at the bottom of the boundary as the lowest O2 that sustains burning of the sample (the fundamental limit), slightly below 14% O2 around 10 cm/s, which it calls considerably lower than conventional-table normal-gravity PMMA LOI and upward values.

At about the same flow, about 9.2 cm/s, the figure has another in-between point at about 13.8% O2 labelled qc 0.51 W/cm2; the figure's mark for this limit is labelled 0.44 W/cm2. qc is the flame's conductive heat loss into the sphere at extinction.

inferred.text: Of these two Fig. 8 points, the one with the larger qc label went out at the lower O2, against SOF-02's general trend, which the paper states holds with a few exceptions; the two labels differ by less than the 20% by which SOF-02 says qc may be uncertain.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: An in-between limit, 4-cm PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity, 101.3 kPa: extinction at about 14.6% O2 and about 9.2 cm/s, quenching or blowoff unclear on video; read from SOF-02 Fig. 8.

answer.not_covered: No SoFIE-GEL extinction limit below about 101 kPa is in the documents.

Near 10 cm/s quenching was difficult to tell from blowoff on video, so SOF-02 plots some such points as open 'in-between' symbols. At intermediate flows it found the boundary by O2 depletion, O2 and flow read at the duct entrance at the extinction instant (±0.25%).

SOF-02 places the in-between points at the bottom of the boundary as the lowest O2 that sustains burning of the sample (the fundamental limit), slightly below 14% O2 around 10 cm/s, which it calls considerably lower than conventional-table normal-gravity PMMA LOI and upward values.

This limit is Fig. 8's highest-O2 in-between point and carries the largest qc label among them, 0.91 W/cm2; the lowest-O2 one, about 13.55% at about 11.5 cm/s, is labelled 0.37 W/cm2. qc is the flame's conductive heat loss into the sphere at extinction.

inferred.text: That ordering fits SOF-02's finding that, with a few exceptions, points with smaller qc tend to stay flammable at lower O2 than neighbouring points; the two points also sit at different flows, about 10.3 and about 11.5 cm/s.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: An in-between limit, 4-cm PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity, 101.3 kPa: extinction at about 14.7% O2 and about 10.3 cm/s, quenching or blowoff unclear on video; read from SOF-02 Fig. 8.

answer.not_covered: No SoFIE-GEL extinction limit below about 101 kPa is in the documents.

answers.question: What does the burn limit SOF-02:nodate:PMMA-STAGNATIONBLOWOFF:12dac2c4 (PMMA, 14.4% O2) mean, and how was it measured?

data.text: A stagnation-blowoff point on SOF-02's Fig. 8: the O2 limit for local blowoff at the stagnation point, about 14.4% O2 at extinction, at about 49.7 cm/s upstream forced flow (both read from the figure); 4-cm PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity, 101.3 kPa (1 ± 0.05 atm).

SOF-02 tells blowoff from quenching by the extinction dynamics: blowoff starts with a hole in the upstream stagnation region, then the flame retreats downstream to extinction. O2 and flow are read at the duct entrance at the extinction instant (±0.25%).

This is SOF-02's own measurement, one of 35 tests near 101.3 kPa, from flow changes or O2 depletion; its test and route are not named. Fig. 8 prints no qc label beside the mark for this limit; SOF-02 leaves qc off where re-used samples had more than two thermocouples exposed to the gas or repeated ignition made the fit questionable.

Near this flow Fig. 8 also has a total (wake) blowoff point, about 13.95% O2 at about 50.5 cm/s. SOF-02 finds two blowoff limits at higher flows: wake blowoff may follow stagnation blowoff after a considerable delay, the flame anchored in the slower, lower-strain wake, so wake-blowoff limiting O2 is lower.

inferred.text: Its values match SOF-03's Case #5, test 1410C (49.68 cm/s, 14.37% O2, heat loss not recorded), so it is probably the same test, not a second result (the team's reading); SOF-03 lists that case at 108.4 kPa (1.07 atm), SOF-02 gives 101.3 kPa (1 ± 0.05 atm) for all Fig. 8 tests.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

data.text: This test: SIBAL fabric between black anodized aluminum baffles 2.0 cm apart, ISS microgravity, about 22% O2, 101.3 kPa, 7 cm/s concurrent flow; it burned, spreading steadily at about 0.83 mm/s (read from a figure).
Below 4.0 cm spacing the spread rate fell as the baffles closed in (7 cm/s series); the authors attribute this to oxygen starvation and conductive heat loss to the baffles.

With black baffles 1.0 cm apart, at the same about 22% O2 and 7 cm/s concurrent flow, no flame spread: one passage says it went out once the ignition energy was removed, another that ignition was not achieved.

At 2.0 cm, the smallest spacing at which a flame spread (7 cm/s series), transparent baffles gave a slightly higher spread rate than the aluminum ones; the authors read this as conductive heat loss to the close baffles, aluminum being expected to draw more heat.

inferred.text: This test's 2.0 cm spacing lies just above the quench limit that Fig. 7 draws at about 1.2 to 1.5 cm (read from a figure), and its spread rate is the lowest of its baffle type in the 7 cm/s series.

other_side.note: at 1.0 cm spacing, same baffle type and flow, no flame spread

lead.text: At 7 cm/s this test burned with baffles 2.0 cm apart, while at 1.0 cm none spread; the authors link slower close-spaced spread to oxygen starvation and baffle heat loss.

With the same baffles 2.0 cm apart, at the same about 22% O2 and 7 cm/s concurrent flow, the fabric burned, spreading steadily at about 0.96 mm/s (read from a figure).

For black baffles 1.0 cm apart at 7 cm/s, another passage says the flame went out right after the ignition energy was removed and never spread past the ignition wire (burn length under 0.8 cm), so the paper's two accounts of the 1.0 cm tests differ.

inferred.text: This test's 1.0 cm spacing lies below the quench limit that Fig. 7 draws at about 1.2 to 1.5 cm (read from a figure).

other_side.note: the same baffle type 2.0 cm apart, same flow, burned

lead.text: At 7 cm/s the paper reports no ignition with baffles 1.0 cm apart, which the authors attribute to reduced oxygen supply and baffle heat loss; at 2.0 cm flames spread.

answer.not_covered: No burn length is reported for this test.

answers.question: Why did test SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-TRANSPARENT-D2.0CM-7CMS:680ab506 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 22% O2) burn?

data.text: This test: SIBAL fabric between transparent polycarbonate baffles 2.0 cm apart, ISS microgravity, about 22% O2, 101.3 kPa, 7 cm/s concurrent flow; it burned, spreading steadily at about 0.96 mm/s (read from a figure).
Below 4.0 cm spacing the spread rate fell as the baffles closed in (7 cm/s series); the authors attribute this to oxygen starvation and conductive heat loss to the baffles.
With the same baffles 1.0 cm apart, at the same about 22% O2 and 7 cm/s concurrent flow, no flame spread: the paper says ignition was not achieved at 1.0 cm.

At 2.0 cm, the smallest spacing at which a flame spread (7 cm/s series), transparent baffles gave a slightly higher spread rate than the aluminum ones; the authors read this as conductive heat loss to the close baffles, aluminum being expected to draw more heat.

inferred.text: This test's 2.0 cm spacing lies just above the quench limit that Fig. 7 draws at about 1.2 to 1.5 cm (read from a figure), and its spread rate is the lowest of its baffle type in the 7 cm/s series.

other_side.note: at 1.0 cm spacing, same baffle type and flow, no flame spread

lead.text: At 7 cm/s this test burned with baffles 2.0 cm apart, while at 1.0 cm none spread; the authors link slower close-spaced spread to oxygen starvation and baffle heat loss.

answer.not_covered: The paper tested this set-up only at the ISS ambient, about 22% O2 and 101.3 kPa.

answers.question: Why did test SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-TRANSPARENT-D3.0CM-7CMS:4817a564 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 22% O2) burn?

data.text: This test: SIBAL fabric between transparent polycarbonate baffles 3.0 cm apart, ISS microgravity, about 22% O2, 101.3 kPa, 7 cm/s concurrent flow; it burned, spreading steadily at about 1.67 mm/s (read from a figure; the figure's three 3.0 cm marks overlap).

At 3.0 cm spacing the three baffle types gave almost identical spread rates (7 cm/s series); the authors take this to suggest that at such confinement burning is limited by the oxygen supplied to the gap between the baffles.

Below 4.0 cm spacing the spread rate fell as the baffles closed in (7 cm/s series), faster than the linear trend Li et al. predicted; the authors attribute this to oxygen starvation and conductive heat loss to the baffles, adding that some flow may have been diverted outside the baffles, lowering the flow between them, especially when close.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: At 7 cm/s this test spread steadily with baffles 3.0 cm apart, where the three baffle types gave almost identical rates; the authors suggest the gap's oxygen supply limits burning.

answer.not_covered: The paper tested this set-up only at the ISS ambient, about 22% O2 and 101.3 kPa.

answers.question: Why did test SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-TRANSPARENT-D4.0CM-7CMS:8fe08993 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 22% O2) burn?

data.text: This test: SIBAL fabric between transparent polycarbonate baffles 4.0 cm apart, ISS microgravity, about 22% O2, 101.3 kPa, 7 cm/s concurrent flow; it burned, spreading steadily at about 1.74 mm/s (read from a figure).
In the 7 cm/s series, spread rate and flame length peaked at 4.0 cm spacing for all three baffle types, the optimal spacing Li et al. had predicted.

At 4.0 cm and 7 cm/s, Fig. 8 shows the flame longest with reflective baffles and slightly shorter with transparent than with black ones; the authors explain that polycarbonate and black aluminum let through or absorb much more radiation, which reflective baffles redirect back.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

answers.question: Why did test SOF-08:nodate:SIBAL-TRANSPARENT-D5.0CM-7CMS:c97e26a1 (SIBAL fabric (75% cotton, 25% fiberglass), 22% O2) burn?

data.text: This test: SIBAL fabric between transparent polycarbonate baffles 5.0 cm apart, ISS microgravity, about 22% O2, 101.3 kPa, 7 cm/s concurrent flow; it burned, spreading steadily at about 1.63 mm/s (read from a figure).

The authors' reading for steady cases: above the optimal spacing (4.0 cm in this work), thermal expansion during combustion accelerates the flow and strengthens conductive heat feedback to the sample, raising the spread rate.

At the same spacing, flame length and spread rate were highest with polished aluminum and lowest with transparent polycarbonate baffles, the differences largest at intermediate spacings; near the limit set by the reduced oxygen supply they were similar for all types per the abstract, while the conclusions say the ranking reverses at quenching.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: At 7 cm/s this test spread steadily with baffles 5.0 cm apart, above the 4.0 cm optimum, where the authors say thermal expansion accelerates the flow and strengthens conductive feedback.

answer.not_covered: The paper tested this set-up only at the ISS ambient, about 22% O2 and 101.3 kPa.

answers.question: Why did test SOFIE-GEL:1402C (PMMA, 13.5% O2) go out?

data.text: Test 1402C: a 4-cm PMMA sphere in ISS microgravity, ignited by a heated coil, inside the duct with the flow held at 11.50 cm/s while O2 fell by natural depletion. Table 1 lists intermediate-mode extinction at 13.54% O2 and 108.4 kPa.

SOF-03 calls it representative of the intermediate-flow tests at 9.22 to 11.5 cm/s: as O2 depleted, the tip shrank without pulsating and the flame went out normally within one video frame, without base pulsation.

SOF-02's map of 35 microgravity tests on 4-cm PMMA spheres at 101 ± 5 kPa puts the bottom of the extinction band, where the blowoff and quenching branches merge, around 10 cm/s, with minimum O2 slightly below 14%.

inferred.text: At 11.50 cm/s and 13.54% O2, test 1402C sits at that band bottom, among the lowest-O2 extinctions these spheres show.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Test 1402C, a PMMA sphere in an 11.50 cm/s flow in orbit, went out as O2 depleted to 13.54%, normally within one video frame: SOF-03's representative intermediate case.

answer.not_covered: The diluent of the test atmosphere is not reported.

answers.question: Why did test SOFIE-GEL:1403B (PMMA, 19.9% O2) go out?

data.text: Test 1403B: a 4-cm PMMA sphere in forced flow in ISS microgravity (CIR), near 101.3 kPa, hot-wire ignited. The flame quenched at 19.9% O2 and 0.84 cm/s in Table 2, 0.85 cm/s in the text, with qc 0.5 W/cm2 after 384 s from ignitor on.

SOF-02 lists this test among its quenching extinctions, which the authors attribute to excessive flame heat loss. They find that less flame heat loss into the sphere (smaller qc, more sub-surface heating) lowers the quench velocity.
Of the three Fig. 6 tests near 20% O2 (1407A, 1407B, 1403B), 1403B had the smallest qc and longest heat-up, and quenched at the lowest flow.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Test 1403B (PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity) quenched at 19.9% O2 and 0.84 cm/s in Table 2, 0.85 in the text; SOF-02 attributes quenching to excessive flame heat loss.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no time history of this test's flow and O2 before extinction.

answers.question: Why did test SOFIE-GEL:1403C (PMMA, 14.4% O2) go out?

data.text: Test 1403C: a 4-cm PMMA sphere in ISS microgravity (CIR), hot-wire ignited at 21 cm/s, 17.74% O2 and 103.5 kPa. At 317.04 s, at 73.3 cm/s and 14.39% O2, the flame blew off locally at the stagnation point; total blowoff followed at 330 s.

SOF-02's Example #2, blowoff by flow increase: inside the duct the flow was raised quickly in steps to 75 cm/s between 250 and 290 s. O2 also depleted, but the flow changed far faster, so SOF-02 treats the flow change as the dominant cause.

After the stagnation hole opened, the flame front retreated and held in the near wake for 15 s while O2 fell from 14.39% to 13.89%. SOF-02 says wake blowoff can follow after a long delay because the flame anchors in the slower, lower-strain wake.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Test 1403C (PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity) blew off at the stagnation point at 73.3 cm/s and 14.39% O2 after a flow increase, which SOF-02 treats as the dominant cause.

answer.not_covered: Flow and O2 at the total blowoff (330 s) are not stated separately.

SOF-02 lists this test among its quenching extinctions, which the authors attribute to excessive flame heat loss. They find that less flame heat loss into the sphere (smaller qc, more sub-surface heating) lowers the quench velocity.

answers.question: Why did test SOFIE-GEL:1407B (PMMA, 20.1% O2) go out?

data.text: Test 1407B: a re-used 4-cm PMMA sphere in ISS microgravity, hot-wire ignited, starting at 17.7 cm/s, 23% O2 and 102.3 kPa. It quenched at 20.14% O2 and 1.32 cm/s in Table 2, 20.1% and 1.25 cm/s in the Example #1 text.

SOF-02's Example #1, quenching by flow decrease: the flow was lowered to 9.7 cm/s at 204 s, then cut in quick steps to 1.25 cm/s from 278 s; the flame tips retreated toward the front stagnation region and pulsed before quenching.
O2 also fell in the sealed chamber, but the flow changed far faster, so SOF-02 treats the flow change as the dominant extinction cause in Examples #1 and #2.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Test 1407B (PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity) quenched at 20.14% O2 after the flow was cut from 17.7 cm/s; SOF-02 treats that flow decrease as the dominant cause.

answer.not_covered: SOF-02 does not state the pressure at the moment of this quench.

answers.question: Why did test SOFIE-GEL:1408A (PMMA, 15% O2) go out?

data.text: Test 1408A: a 4-cm PMMA sphere in ISS microgravity, ignited by a heated coil, inside the duct with the flow held at 34.28 cm/s while O2 fell by natural depletion. Table 1 lists blowoff at 14.99% O2 and 107.4 kPa.

Extinction began with a flame hole at the stagnation point, a local blowoff once O2 dropped below 14.99% at this strain rate of 25.7 s−1; after two base pulsation cycles the flame spun around the sphere for 3.18 s before complete blowoff.
SOF-03 holds that blowoff at high speed comes from short residence time in the flame stabilisation zone, heat loss modifying its boundary only modestly.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Test 1408A, a PMMA sphere in a 34.28 cm/s flow in orbit, began to blow off as O2 depleted to 14.99%; SOF-03 ties high-speed blowoff to short residence time.

answer.not_covered: SOF-03 does not print the O2 at complete blowoff.

answers.question: Why did test SOFIE-GEL:1409B (PMMA, 14.2% O2) go out?

data.text: Test 1409B: a 4-cm PMMA sphere in ISS microgravity, hot-wire ignited at 17.2 cm/s, 19.1% O2 and 102.3 kPa; inside the duct the flow was held at 4.7 cm/s from 271 s. It quenched at 14.21% O2, 4.83 cm/s and 104.9 kPa.

This is SOF-02's Example #3, quenching by O2 depletion at an intermediate flow: because the flow stayed constant, the authors attribute the quench to O2 depletion in the sealed chamber. From about 740 s the tip retreated upstream in larger-amplitude pulsation cycles.
SOF-03 reports the same test as its Case #1 (inside the duct, 4.83 cm/s, 14.21% O2) and counts ten complete cycles of tip pulsation and retreat before quenching.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Test 1409B (PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity) quenched at 14.21% O2 and 4.83 cm/s; because the flow was held constant, SOF-02 attributes the quench to O2 depletion.

answer.not_covered: The diluent of the test atmosphere is not reported.

answers.question: Why did test SOFIE-GEL:1409C (PMMA, 20.8% O2) go out?

data.text: Test 1409C: a 4-cm PMMA sphere at the duct exit in ISS microgravity, ignited by a heated coil; nominal flow cut to 0.4 cm/s at 309 s, then 0.2 cm/s. Table 1 lists quenching at 20.77% O2, 0.44 cm/s and 104.4 kPa.
From 311 s the tip pulsed for 927 s until quenching at 1237.88 s as O2 depleted from 26.25% to 20.77%; SOF-03 calls it self-sustained and expects it would have lasted longer without depletion.

SOF-03 holds that at low stretch, with long residence time or large standoff, quenching occurs once heat loss becomes a significant fraction of heat release and cools the flame enough to extinguish it.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Test 1409C, a PMMA sphere in ultra-low flow in orbit, pulsed 927 s and quenched at 0.44 cm/s as O2 depleted to 20.77%; SOF-03 links low-stretch quenching to heat loss.

answer.not_covered: No SoFIE-GEL limits below about 101 kPa are reported.

answers.question: Why did test SOFIE-GEL:1410A (PMMA, 16% O2) go out?

data.text: Test 1410A: a 4-cm PMMA sphere in forced flow in ISS microgravity (CIR), near 101.3 kPa, hot-wire ignited. The flame quenched at 16.01% O2 and 4.71 cm/s, read at the duct entrance, with qc 0.75 W/cm2 after 320 s from ignitor on.

SOF-02 lists this test among its quenching extinctions, which the authors attribute to excessive flame heat loss. They find that less flame heat loss into the sphere (smaller qc, more sub-surface heating) lowers the quench O2.
Its Fig. 7 partner 1409B, at a similar flow (4.83 cm/s), had a smaller qc after 717 s of heat-up and quenched lower, at 14.21% O2 and 104.9 kPa.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Test 1410A (PMMA sphere, ISS microgravity) quenched at 16.01% O2 and 4.71 cm/s; SOF-02 attributes quenching to excessive flame heat loss and finds less heat loss lowers the quench O2.

answer.not_covered: The documents give no flow or O2 history of this test, so how it was driven to extinction is not stated.

answers.question: Why did test SOFIE-GEL:1410C (PMMA, 14.4% O2) go out?

data.text: Test 1410C: a 4-cm PMMA sphere at the duct exit in ISS microgravity, ignited by a heated coil, flow held at 49.68 cm/s while O2 depleted. Table 1 lists blowoff at 14.37% O2 and 108.4 kPa, the envelope flame's O2 before local blowoff.

Local blowoff opened a hole at the front stagnation region; the flame restabilised at the sphere's shoulder and lasted 40 s, spinning for about 35 s, breaking into flamelets as O2 fell to 13.89% at 423.30 s.
SOF-03 explains the end: as more surface is exposed it cools until it no longer releases enough fuel vapour to keep burning.

other_side.note: no opposing evidence in the documents

lead.text: Test 1410C, a PMMA sphere in 49.68 cm/s flow in orbit, blew off locally near 14.37% O2, burned at its shoulder 40 s; SOF-03 attributes the end to surface cooling.

answer.not_covered: SOF-03 does not print the O2 at final extinction.
